beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new; this is the module title.

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing means handing over context, a skill, output or an interface, and the real obstacle is whether people take it up.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: I should have a story ready. Our CRM dashboards fit, nobody opens them.

beats.trigger: **Select** the smallest shareable form (share context / share a skill / share the output / share an interface) for the outcome the teammate wants moved
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a list of verbs, but 'smallest shareable form' is a useful phrase.

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I thought of Mikko in pricing. I hesitate because he'd see my setup as extra work, not help.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not from my agent. I accept this, though it's close to what I'd already say as a strategy person.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: There's a test for whether the job statement is specific. I can check that quickly, and the interrupt lines help when the agent reads too widely or too shallowly.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: I should pick the sharing shape by the outcome, not by what we have. It's a good rule, and I've seen platform-first picks before.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a handoff to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: The next step is to find the main obstacle and write a technical plan and a people plan.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Look for the one obstacle that sits behind the others. That is how I'd structure a consulting problem, and here I can check it against my own team.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: The empty people plan is the real result. I'd expect mine to be full of UNASSIGNED, and that's the useful part for my fourteen.

beats.trigger: writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a pointer to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until a person has tested them.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: This is the question that tests whether Mikko would actually switch. It also gives me something to say to the pricing working group.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: Imagine the failure first, then turn the strongest one into one conversation and one test. It's a pre-mortem, and it fits.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Pick against the outcome, not the tooling. That's a sentence I can reuse in my own meetings.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a lead-in to the lecture.

beats.trigger: The interview earned its keep when it found a third outcome past speed and quality: a dependency removed, an anxiety gone, a scope widened.
beats.got: If the interview only finds speed and quality, it was too shallow. Look for a third thing, like a dependency or an anxiety. That is a useful check.

beats.trigger: They run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: The agent file is only a shell. The value sits in the memory and the corrections that lived with the builder. This is exactly what would happen if I forwarded my setup to my team.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily. Accountability stays with whoever built it. Good line, but it takes a long time to get there.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Nothing new. Access is not usage. We already know that from licence dashboards.

beats.trigger: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: People take up what resembles their own work. Polanyi is nice, but it makes the same point again in different words.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: The interface is the first piece that depends on another person. It's a little abstract and I don't need it.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A good analysis got no decision because the people deciding had not done the work themselves. I recognise this from my pricing pilot and my CFO. It's the best part of the module and I'd bring my own version.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: The conditions for switching are small and specific: it lands where they already look, it's right the first time, and someone they trust vouches for it. This is what I'll use.

beats.trigger: What you learned getting here is not one of the four things.
beats.got: Whether they pick it up is their decision. That's fair but already said. The last sentence is cryptic.

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet
beats.got: The people plan stalls on names, and that gap is the unfinished part. The small move is one name.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent sharpens the sharing file and I push back where it's wrong. Fine, but it's a routine step.

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
beats.got: Challenge the summary and save the conversation. Nothing new.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true for them to switch?
beats.got: nothing new; a recap of the four points.

beats.trigger: Test one assumption. Ask for one name. Talk to one person.
beats.got: I have to bring one tested assumption and one named person. That is concrete, and it's the only homework I'd actually do.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new; Module 8 builds on what comes back.

take_homes: Start from the teammate's job, not my setup. A shared agent file is only a shell. The value sits in the memory and corrections, and in someone who answers for it.
Ask 'what would have to be true for them to switch?' It has to land where they already look, be right the first time, and have someone they trust vouching for it.
The people plan is where I'll stall, because it needs names. An empty slot is the real finding. The leadership story is a warning: a good analysis goes nowhere if the decider didn't do the work.

monday.move: Interview Mikko about how he does the usage-pricing analysis today, then ask which of the pilot-cohort brief inputs he'd trust. Also write down the three or four context files my team currently keeps as private copies and propose one shared place for them.
monday.who: Mikko (pricing working group) first, then my fourteen
monday.when: Monday morning, 30 minutes with Mikko before the pricing working group sync
monday.stop_condition: If Mikko can't name how he does the job today or what would make him switch, I stop building and ask again. I also don't ship the brief to the working group until one person other than me has used it.
monday.blocker: No shared home for the context files, and nobody owns it yet. The owner slot in my people plan is probably UNASSIGNED.

misconception.why: The module never says prompts don't matter, but the point that the work lives in memory, corrections and judgement rather than in the agent file undercuts 'better prompts' as the goal. I'm not fully convinced. I still think prompting skill is part of it.

one_line: The exercises are good because they make you name a person and a failure. The lecture repeats itself in the middle, but the story about the analysis nobody decided on is worth the hour.
